problems.description: Table initialization is done via a before_request hook gated by an `app.db_initialized` attribute — a lazy-init hack. Schema creation should run once at startup inside an app context (e.g., in __main__ or a CLI command); the per-request check adds overhead and the attribute mutation is not thread-safe across workers.
Module-level `db_path` in app.py is lowercase; measurement flags module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE (the only in-diff occurrence of the 8 reported violations).
New route handlers (`create_task`, `list_tasks`, `get_task`, `update_task`) dropped the type hints present on the original functions, regressing the repo's public-signature typing convention.
Adds a flask_sqlalchemy dependency; the diff shows no requirements.txt update to record it, leaving the new import unvendored.

Test fixture mutates `app.config['SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI']` after `db` was already bound to the app; depending on Flask-SQLAlchemy version the engine may already be cached, so tests may not actually hit the in-memory DB.
`datetime.utcnow` is deprecated in Python 3.12; new code should use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`.
PUT silently ignores empty-string `title`/`status` instead of validating, which is inconsistent with the 400 validation on POST.

strengths: Fixes a genuine correctness bug: the original seed INSERT hardcoded status 'done' while returning 'pending'; the ORM version writes and returns 'pending' consistently.
Net quality improvement confirmed mechanically: smells −2, bugs +0, duplications 0.0%, cognitive complexity +0.
Removes dead code (`_legacy_format_date`, `_notify_admin` stubs) and the stale module docstring.
Adds a comprehensive 236-line pytest suite covering success, 400/404 paths, and PUT updates with in-memory DB isolation.
Respects the existing single-file structure, endpoint semantics, and response codes (200/201/400/404); absolute sqlite path is more robust than the relative `todos.db`.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid greenfield modernization that fixes a real status bug, removes dead code, and adds a full test suite (net 'better', smells −2), but relies on a before_request lazy-init hack and drops type hints; note the measured 0.71 convention score overstates this commit's blame since 5 of the 8 flagged violations (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py) fall outside this diff.

problems.description: JWT_SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-key-change-in-production' value, so a misconfigured deployment would silently accept forgeable tokens; the app should fail fast or require the env var in production.
8 convention violations (module-level constants not UPPER_CASE, snake_case/PascalCase issues in celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_api.py) drive convention score to 0.71.
Cognitive complexity +19 concentrated in the token_required decorator and auth handlers; token extraction/validation could be extracted into a helper.
Stateless JWTs are not invalidated on password change and there is no logout/revocation mechanism; acceptable for a demo app but worth noting.

strengths: Passwords are hashed via werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash, never stored or returned in plaintext.
Owner-scoped access control is enforced consistently across create/list/get/update routes via the token_required decorator.
The decorator-based auth follows existing Flask route and error-handling idioms in app.py, integrating cleanly with the current structure.
Solid test coverage added for registration and login, including validation and error paths.
commit_reviews.summary: This is a net-positive feature_addition that fits the task-manager architecture well — clean owner scoping, hashed passwords, and decorator-based auth with tests — though it carries minor debt from a hardcoded dev secret fallback and a sub-par convention score of 0.71 driven largely by naming-rule violations.

problems.description: send_notification_email.delay() is invoked unguarded inside the request handler; if the Celery broker (Redis) is unavailable the dispatch raises and PUT /tasks/{id} returns 500, coupling the core task-update path to notification infrastructure. Notification failure should never break the primary write path.
tasks.py emits both logger.info and a print() statement for the same event; redundant output channels in production code (print belongs only in a demo/CLI, not the async task).

Measured convention score 0.71 with 8 violations, mainly module-level constants not UPPER_CASE (broker_url, result_backend, logger, db_path). The snake_case/PascalCase flags in celery_config.py and tasks.py appear to be analyzer false positives since those files define no user functions/classes — flagging the discrepancy per instructions.

Introduces hard runtime dependencies on Celery and a Redis broker; the visible diff shows no requirements.txt update and no worker startup/queue provisioning, so the feature is only functional once infrastructure is supplied externally.

All five tests patch .delay(), so the real task body and broker interaction are never exercised; fine for unit coverage, but a session labeled 'integration' does not verify the actual worker path or the mocked print/log behavior.

strengths: Notification dispatch is scoped precisely to the old_status != 'completed' -> completed transition, avoiding spurious emails on unrelated updates and duplicate-complete re-triggers.
Clean separation of concerns: celery_config.py (broker config), tasks.py (async work), app.py (dispatch via .delay()) keeps async concerns out of the request handler.

Five focused tests cover trigger, email passthrough, no-trigger on other status changes, idempotent duplicate-complete, and combined title+status update; SonarQube reports +0 bugs and dispatch happens after commit (no commit/broker race).
Broker and result backend are configured from environment variables with sane defaults and the task is routed to a dedicated 'notifications' queue.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-separated and well-tested integration session that adds Celery-based notifications with correct edge-case handling, though it leaves an unguarded .delay() dispatch on the request path and carries mostly cosmetic casing convention violations (measured convention 0.71, with snake_case/PascalCase flags in the new modules appearing to be analyzer false positives).

problems.description: Repository subclasses duplicate the base class: create_user/create_task reimplement BaseRepository.create and update_task reimplements BaseRepository.update (only differing in how None-args are handled), inflating cognitive complexity by +8 and undercutting the abstraction's value.

register() now calls generate_password_hash() directly in the route, bypassing the model's set_password() encapsulation. Hashing responsibility leaks from the model layer into the controller, and the diff shows no corresponding import for the new call.

BaseRepository.update() silently skips any kwarg whose value is None, so a field can never be intentionally cleared; update_task() also re-fetches the task via get_by_id even though the route already fetched it for the ownership check, adding a redundant query per request.

Measured convention score is 0.71 with 8 violations, but most (celery_config.py, tasks.py, test_api.py) are pre-existing in files untouched by this commit; the new repositories.py itself follows naming conventions cleanly (PascalCase classes, snake_case methods).

strengths: Centralizes persistence behind a repository layer, removing scattered Model.query calls from route handlers and reducing duplication by 0.2% (measured).
No new bugs or code smells reported by SonarQube; core query semantics and error contracts (401/404/409 JSON responses, ownership checks) are preserved.
Clean structure and naming: BaseRepository abstraction with concrete UserRepository/TaskRepository, leaving routes thin and declarative.
commit_reviews.summary: Sound repository-layer refactor that centralizes persistence and cuts duplication with no new bugs or smells, but it undercuts its own abstraction by duplicating base-class methods in subclasses and leaking password hashing into the route layer.

problems.description: Fail-open rate limiting: bare `except Exception` around Limiter init silently swaps in NoOpLimiter, disabling a security control when Redis is unreachable. Should fail closed (or log loudly) instead of quietly dropping rate limits.

test_api.py fixture uses bare `except: pass` around Redis flushdb() and introduces an external Redis (localhost:6379) dependency; tests silently skip rate-limit isolation if Redis is down, making results nondeterministic across environments.

Redundant rate limiting: `default_limits=["100 per minute"]` plus identical `@limiter.limit("100 per minute")` on every route duplicates the same policy in two places, so tuning limits requires editing every decorator.
New module-level constants `redis_url` and `redis_client` are lowercase, matching the reported UPPER_CASE convention violations; should be `REDIS_URL`/`REDIS_CLIENT`.
`get_tasks_paginated` runs `query.count()` on every page, an O(n) full scan per request that scales poorly with task count; acceptable for the story tier but not a long-term pattern.
The GET /tasks response shape changes from a bare array to an envelope object, a breaking contract change for any existing consumers.

strengths: Per-user rate limit keying via JWT user_id is a more precise control than IP-based limiting.
Cursor-based pagination is correctly placed in TaskRepository with limit+1 overflow detection and a stable id cursor.
Repository/controller layering respected: pagination logic lives in the data layer, routes stay thin.
Tests updated comprehensively to the new response contract, with Redis flush to isolate rate-limit state.
commit_reviews.summary: Cross-cutting commit that adds genuinely useful, well-layered rate limiting and cursor pagination and improves the codebase overall, but carries debt in a fail-open limiter fallback, a bare-except Redis dependency in tests, and a few naming/redundancy slips.

compounding_issues: The S2 'legacy' compatibility-user migration (reassigning unowned tasks) became permanent carry-forward complexity that every later session had to preserve and re-implement (moved into UserRepository.initialize_database in S4).
Idempotent ALTER TABLE migrations (owner_id, then email) accumulated inside init_db across sessions, creating a brittle forward-only migration chain rather than a schema-versioning strategy.
JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'development-secret-change-me' value throughout all sessions — a security debt never addressed.

S5 switched list ordering from created_at DESC (S1-S4) to id DESC for cursor pagination and changed the GET /tasks response shape (array → {data, next_cursor, total}), a breaking API change introduced late.
Both Celery (S3) and Flask-Limiter (S5) hardcode Redis on localhost:6379, coupling runtime behavior to a local Redis daemon with only an in-memory fallback for rate limits.
key_decisions: S2 introduced JWT authentication with per-user task ownership (owner_id column + 'legacy' user reassignment migration) — every subsequent session routes through the require_auth decorator.
S4 extraction of a repository layer (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository), shrinking app.py ~126 lines and cleanly enabling S5's pagination.
S3 Celery integration for async completion notifications (celery_config.py + tasks.py), the only external-service decision.
Idempotent schema evolution via PRAGMA table_info column checks before ALTER TABLE, used consistently across S2-S4.
S5 cursor-based pagination + Redis-backed per-user rate limiting as the final cross-cutting hardening layer.
S1 hardened the seed: timezone-aware datetimes, strict input validation, init_db() at import time, and a proper pytest suite with tmp_path fixtures.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across all five sessions with no degradation or rewrites. S1 hardened the raw seed (timezone-aware timestamps, strict validation, import-time init, first test suite), S2 added a well-designed JWT auth and ownership model with a careful data migration, S3 integrated Celery cleanly behind the existing model layer, S4 refactored data access into a clean repository layer that shrank app.py by half, and S5 topped the arc with production cross-cutting concerns (Redis-backed rate limiting and cursor pagination) while updating the test suite to match. The test suite grew from 3 to 9 passing tests, and the codebase's seam quality improved each session, though early migration machinery and a hardcoded dev secret carried forward as persistent technical debt.
story_review.summary: A textbook incremental build where each session composes on the prior with no dead ends — greenfield hardening to auth to async integration to refactor to cross-cutting hardening — producing a coherent, well-tested API whose quality rises steadily across all five commits.
